This research paper considers a control problem that involves a random evolution equation and includes the presence of a stochastic parameter that changes over time. A new numerical scheme is developed to solve this problem, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through the analysis of its errors. A comparison with an alternative method known as the Galerkin-Green method shows that under certain conditions, the new scheme yields superior results in terms of accuracy. A stability and convergence analysis are also performed, and these are reflected in the paper's theorems 1 and 2. The author has previously published results similar to theorems 1 and 2 in the journal Nonlinear Analysis: Hybrid Systems, under the paper title Numerical Resolution of a Control Issue for a Semilinear Evolution Equation with Delay and Random Parameters. The current paper provides an expanded version of the results found in [2] and includes an error estimation and an order of convergence. The author also notes that the conditions presented in the paper can be applied to the model studied in [2] and will result in a more general error estimation theorem. The numerical scheme developed in this paper can be viewed as a variation of the method known as the Euler-Maruyama method, and it involves the use of a random test function. The author has previously published results on the method known as the Euler-Maruyama method in the journal Evolution Equations and Control Theory, under the paper title Weakly Stationary Feedback Control of a Stochastic Camassa-Holm Equation. The numerical scheme developed in this paper will yield a random and weakly stationary discretization of the control problem, and this will result in the scheme's being tested using the H\"{o}lder regularity property. The author has previously published results on the H\"{o}lder regularity property in the journal Nonlinear Analysis: Hybrid Systems, under the paper title Numerical Resolution of a Control Issue for a Semilinear Evolution Equation with Delay and Random Parameters. The development of the numerical scheme is also viewed as a variation of the method known as the Galerkin method known as the Galerkin-Euler method, and this involves the use of a random test function. The scheme known as the Galerkin-Euler method includes the presence of the parameter $\Delta t$ in the terms known as the diffusion and convection terms, and this results in the scheme's being able to solve the problem even when the solution's H\"{o}lder regularity is less than $1/2$. Our recent comprehensive study of the Pierre Auger Observatory's most energetic cosmic rays has uncovered significant patterns of anisotropy in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.  Our findings show that the most energetic cosmic rays exhibit a preference for vertical arrival directions during the day side of the Earth, a phenomenon that vanishes at lower energies.  We have also discovered two major anisotropy regions in the Northern Hemisphere: a network of highly significant cosmic-ray clusters centered around the constellation Telescopium, and a less pronounced pattern in the Southern Hemisphere.  Our studies suggest that these anisotropies are likely the result of intermediate-scale magnetic fields influencing the path of high-energy cosmic rays over long distances.  We estimate these cosmic rays possess energies in the range of 20-60 EeV and advocate for further studies with larger detectors that can fully capture the anisotropies of the most energetic cosmic rays.  Our research underscores the significance of large-aperture detectors like the AugerArray, which would be capable of fully capturing these anisotropies and other phenomena crucial for understanding high-energy cosmic rays.  The Telescopium anisotropy appears to be stable over the observed time frame but our study was unable to establish a temporal pattern for the Southern Hemisphere anisotropy.  Our current understanding suggests that the most energetic cosmic rays primarily originate from nearby active galactic nuclei that emit jets, but we were unable to tie the Telescopium or Southern Hemisphere anisotropies to specific AGN sources.  The lack of correlation between the right ascension of the most energetic cosmic rays and the Milky Way's center also supports the idea that the most energetic cosmic rays can reach Earth from a wide range of directions and suggests that the most energetic cosmic rays are likely the higher-energy tail of a population that can be described by a single distribution, rather than multiple populations.  The extensive anisotropies we observed will serve as a vital benchmark for any future detector seeking to understand the origins of the most energetic cosmic rays.  The AugerArray, with its larger aperture and ability to study the most energetic cosmic rays through the Pierre Auger Observatory, would be well-suited for fully capturing the anisotropies of the most energetic cosmic rays and has the potential to significantly advance our understanding of these enigmatic particles.  The collaborative nature of the AugerArray's design would also facilitate real-time data analysis and facilitate the discovery of transient phenomena among the most energetic cosmic rays.

Our research examines the relationship between particle pair's azimuthal angle and their relative momentum, studying the most forward and mid-rapidity regions of Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV.  We compared the observed patterns to theoretical models, analyzing the effects of collective flow and examining the differences in particle pair's motion.  Our findings show that the majority of particles' motion can be explained by collective flow, with the average transverse velocity of particles decreasing with increasing distance from the collision axis.  We also calculated the average transverse velocity of particles, finding that it depends on the collision's impact parameter and decreases with increasing energy.  However, we found a discrepancy between our results and the theoretical predictions of ALISA-QCD, which may be attributed to the collision energy or the influence of the collision axis on particle pair's motion.  Additionally, we found that the majority of forward-rapidity particles move in the same direction as the collision axis, which cannot be accounted for by collective flow alone.  We propose several possible explanations for this phenomenon, including the effects of initial conditions, hydrodynamic turbulence, and charge-alignment.  We also extracted information about the properties of the system's initial state, deriving the distribution of the angular velocity of particles and finding that it agrees with the predictions of initial conditions that are derived from hydrodynamic simulations.  We further investigated the differences between particle pairs that move in the same direction as the collision axis and those that move in opposite directions, finding that the majority of particles that move in opposite directions have higher momentum than those that move in the same direction. We introduce a method for managing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Our approach, designed to accommodate the common format of relational tables used in knowledge base representation, incorporates two key features. Firstly, we use a novel format that combines tables with functional relationships, and secondly, we develop an algorithm to repair inconsistent tables to different levels of consistency, utilizing either primary key-based repairs or table-wide repairs in the presence of functional relationships. Our method can also determine if a given instance satisfies a set of data constraints expressed using first-order logic. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to real-world datasets and benchmark tests. Furthermore, we show that our method's performance in repair tasks and query answering can be compared to established benchmarks, offering insights into its strengths and limitations. Our approach, along with example code and datasets, is available online for public use.

The time-varying Poisson autoregressive model has gained popularity in modeling discrete time series data. Although several variants exist, such as with external regressors, with constraints, and with changes in parameters, research on temporal changes within models of type 2 order has been limited. This study develops a first-order time-varying Poisson autoregressive model and explores its properties, including statistical convergence and consistency. Additionally, we compare its performance to a switching model using synthetic data and conduct an exploratory analysis of real data. The results indicate that the model can adapt to data characteristics, and even perform well when compared to a switching model, however the need for further development, particularly in estimating the temporal component, becomes apparent. This research offers an initial step towards exploring the time-varying Poisson autoregressive model of type 2 order and provides several potential directions for future study. Our novel Neural Description Fields construct an object representation that can be used in tasks like navigation and manipulation within cluttered environments. These representations are based on object descriptions and combine the benefits of grid-based neural networks and differential equations. Specifically, we demonstrate how Neural Description Fields can effectively manage complex object representations by breaking them down into simpler components, and how their invariant properties can be exploited to reduce the amount of data required for training. In addition, we show that these fields can be combined with control systems to guide robots in finding specific objects, and our experiments with a Baxter robot in a simulated environment show significant improvements over the current state-of-the-art. Our code is available at https://github.com/ethz-assistant-systems/ndf_baxter.

This abstract representation allows us to identify edge critical behavior's basic requirements and categorize it within the universality classes defined by the parameters' ratios. Our results have implications for theories that exhibit Yang-Lee edge singularity and provide a framework for predicting whether edge critical behavior will occur in these theories. Our research also offers a novel perspective on the universality classes defined by the parameters' ratios and surface field theory. Moreover, we discuss the model's extensions and the edge singularity's properties in $d$-dimensional space–time. The approach we've taken has been shown to be effective in similar contexts and could be relevant for other models and theories. This in turn implies that the fluctuations of the magnetization are confined to a narrow range, consistent with the results of our previous studies on the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model at its critical temperature. While assessing the effects of a global pandemic, the SD-COVID-19 project implemented a rapid response observation campaign to study the aerosol-based spread of disease. This campaign utilized a newly developed, easily constructed instrument to quantify aerosol levels via photometry, employing a simple scattering principle to detect particles of 1-10 microns at wavelengths between 400-700 nanometers. The instrument, called a Scattering Extinction Instrument for COVID (SEI-COVID), was highly effective, with a signal-to-noise ratio of 1000:1 and the ability to detect a 1% change in particle levels. Over a year, 30 nights of data were collected under non-twilight conditions, allowing the team to create a comprehensive, publicly available database of aerosol quantification for 64 to 670 nanometers in breadth, spanning various locations, at multiple sites in India, Nepal, and the Himalayas. By incorporating a novel approach that utilizes the real part of a complex refractive index, the researchers were able to accurately determine the refractive index of atmospheric aerosols, concluding it is similar to that of pollen, with a slight variation in the real component. This finding challenges a long-held assumption that the real component of the index remains constant, and has implications for various remote-sensing applications, including the retrieval of cloud properties from satellite data. Furthermore, the team developed a simple, linear model to predict the signal of the instrument from a distance, allowing them to create a interactive map of the aerosol situation in Kathmandu, Nepal, and surrounding areas. This approach can be applied to other locations, and the team also explored the relationship between aerosol levels and atmospheric temperature, discovering a direct correlation that could have broader implications for the study of aerosols. The data collected during this project is a valuable contribution to the scientific community, and the team believes that the approach used here can be adapted for other research projects, such as studying combustion, wildfires, and volcanic eruptions, as well as Terra and Aqua satellite mission calibration. The code and data for this project are available at https://github.com/SD-COVID-19/SEI-COVID. The team invites collaboration and feedback from the community. In applications like augmented reality, 3D objects' pose needs to be accurately determined from 2D images. Overcoming pose ambiguity requires at least two images of the same scene. In this research, we propose an innovative two-image pose determination framework, known as DeepHMap++, to fully recover 3D scenes' poses. This method integrates projection clustering and correspondence learning through a novel, two-stage process. Initially, two separate neural networks assign cluster IDs to corresponding image pixels based on the projections, and another network trains these IDs to determine poses. Through systematic evaluations, our proposed method was found to outperform the current state-of-the-art in two-image pose determination tasks, especially in scenarios with low resolution images. Additionally, DeepHMap++'s clustered representation was shown to effectively handle complex scenes by successfully determining poses in scenes with numerous objects, whereas existing methods struggled to do so. The code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyangz/DeepHMap++.

This library provides an interface for solving regularized linear inverse problems and Graphical Lasso, and includes tools for estimating parameters and constructing confidence intervals for the underlying graph. Our work builds upon existing research by [d'Alché-Bucy, et al. 2020] and offers novel contributions, specifically the application of the Graphical Lasso to inverse problems with normal-gamma priors. This leads to a derivation of the Generalized Graphical Lasso and associated inference methods. We have made GGLasso an open-source library to facilitate further development and incorporation of newly published methods. This repository can be found at https://github.com/JulienDAlcheBucy/GGLasso. This work was presented at the 2022 ICASSP conference in a paper titled "Generalized Graphical Lasso with Normal-Gamma Priors". This paper is also available online at [arXiv:2106.04987]. This version of GGLasso includes five methods for solving the Generalized Graphical Lasso: Quasi-Newton, Iterative Thresholding, BPDN, FISTA, and Coordinate Descent. To accurately simulate complex biomolecular processes, it is essential to account for configurational fluctuations. However, accurately sampling configurational space while maintaining efficient computation poses a significant challenge. To this end, we derive an improved method for numerically resolving Langevin dynamics, reducing computational noise while boosting the precision of configurational sampling, we achieve this by employing an optimized algorithm for a specific type of dynamics, specifically the velocity-verlet method, our results indicate a 10-fold improvement in precision for the sampling of a standard protein, our approach has been successfully applied to simulate the unfolding of a specific TPC protein and the diffusion of an ion channel, it has the potential to be highly beneficial for time-dependent simulations. Our algorithm has been implemented in the Gromacs molecular dynamics software framework under the name 'langevin-io'.

Research on complex networks often overlooks important details about a system's intricacy by reducing multi-layer networks to single-layer representations based on combined nodes and connections. However, such approaches can cause significant loss of critical information, leading to misinterpretation of vital patterns and prominent eigenvalues in graph theory, including the prominent eigenvector of networks. In this paper, a novel approach is introduced that enables the computation of significant eigenvectors in multi-layer networks, taking into account the interaction between layers, and a general formula is derived to achieve this task. It is demonstrated that this approach can be applied to a wide range of models by examining three examples: networks with alternating pattern of node significance, networks with diverse layers, and network with time-dependent node significance, and it is found that the approach can successfully capture the change in eigenvector prominence with varying parameters. Furthermore, it is shown that the approach can be connected to existing theories by re-expressing the formula in terms of combined networks, allowing for comparison with existing results. In addition, a discussion is presented on the relationship between the approach and combined networks, including the concept of prominence-weighted networks, and it is demonstrated that the approach can preserve the key properties of combined networks, including the property of positive semi-definiteness. A numerical example is also provided to compare the approach with the method of combining networks, showing that the approach can retain the precision of combined networks while avoiding their limitations. A Python code is available for the sake of clarity. It is hoped that this approach will facilitate better understanding and generalization of existing models, as well as inspiring future research on the dynamics of eigenvector prominence in complex networks. It is also proposed to extend the approach to other important eigenvalues in network theory, such as the second eigenvector, and to investigate the relationship between the approach and other measures of node significance, such as centrality measures. In $R$-Minkowski spacetimes, we have discovered a novel $R$-adapted geometric approach, 
which allows us to rephrase Dirac's formula utilizing only the covariant curvature 
operator and the covariant Ricci operator. This formulation serves as an 
alternative to the conventional approach using the Ricci operator and the Bel-Robinson 
tensor. This $R$-geometry framework also enables us to derive Dirac's formula in 
spacetimes with vanishing Ricci tensor. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in the absence 
of a Ricci tensor, the contraction of the Bel-Robinson tensor is consistently zero, 
which is in agreement with the findings of Bieri and the general $R$-Covariant Hamiltonian 
variational formulation. This is also consistent with the findings of Bieri. Additionally,
we propose a novel $R$-geometry interpretation of the Bondi mass aspect change in the 
absence of a Ricci tensor. This involves the derivation of the mass aspect change 
equation using only the Bel-Robinson tensor and the Riemann curvature tensor, which 
results in the well-known mass aspect change equation found by Bieri. This was 
previously obtained using a Hamiltonian variational formulation. This paper can be seen 
as a sequel to the groundbreaking work by Bieri in 2014. This work was presented at 
the GR 19 Conference held in Seoul, Korea in 2019 and the 12th Conference on Recent

This study examines how spheres interact with a liquid surface at moderate speeds, specifically in a seal scenario where the liquid forms a concave surface around the sphere. Our research involves reviewing existing work on this subject, particularly the regime where a crater forms around the sphere. We have conducted these experiments at 1.7m/s for water and 0.5m/s for glycerin using high-speed cameras to capture the surrounding air and the liquid surface. Our results show that reducing the air pressure above the liquid increases the chances of a concave seal, while decreasing the fluid pressure has the opposite effect. We have also established that the shape of the concave seal becomes more spherical as the air pressure increases. In water, this shape turns into a partial crater before eventually becoming a full crater at higher speeds. In glycerin, the shape changes from a concave seal to a partial crater. A well-known hypothesis posits that the fundamental laws of physics must be symmetric under a change of parity, given that the universe appears the same when viewed from opposite sides of any point. While this hypothesis holds true for the standard model of particle physics, it is not a requirement for all possible theories that are consistent with the behavior of particles and the properties of light. In the context of a hypothetical theory known as an effective field theory at a low energy level, researchers found that they could test the validity of this hypothesis by studying the interactions of three particles at high energy levels. By conducting such an analysis on a dataset derived from scattering events, they were able to verify that the hypothesis is indeed a feature of the standard model but not a necessity for the underlying fundamental laws of physics. In the standard model, this necessity is met by a mathematical construct known as a theta-term, which is a means of incorporating a specific aspect of the behavior of particles and the properties of light but is not inherently connected to the symmetry of the universe. The research revealed that the fundamental laws of physics could take the form of a modified version of the standard model, in which the necessity for a certain level of symmetry breaks down at high energy levels, and is guaranteed by a different version of the theta-term known as an extended theta-term. The effectiveness of this form of the standard model in describing the behavior of particles and the properties of light was tested over a wide range of energy levels, from levels as low as a few hundred giga-electronvolts to levels as high as a few hundred teraelectronvolts, and was found to be consistent with the data derived from scattering events. The research also revealed that the fundamental laws of physics could take the form of a modified version of the standard model, in which the necessity for a certain level of symmetry breaks down at low energy levels, and is guaranteed by a different version of the theta-term known as an extended theta-term, but this form of the standard model does not provide a satisfactory description of the behavior of particles and the properties of light at low energy levels. The research has implications for the types of theories that could underlie the standard model and has constraints on the possible energy levels at which the fundamental laws of physics may change in a way that could affect the behavior of particles and the properties of light. Code-mixed languages, which combine scripts from different languages within the same text, are a common means of communication for multilingual individuals across the world, particularly on the internet. This paper explores the challenges of NLP systems when encountering texts in code-mixed languages and the potential benefits of developing these models for benefitting multilingual communities. We outline potential factors hindering NLP performance in this context and discuss several opportunities for addressing them, including designing suitable evaluation metrics, identifying code-mixing's underlying syntax and semantics, and incorporating social context into models, as well as the broader implications for making these models more effective in everyday life. We also touch on the possibility of developing a unified framework for treating different code-mixed languages and offer a preliminary attempt at crafting such a framework for at least two languages, Hindi-English. We hope this work will serve as a starting point for propelling NLP research forward and facilitating more effective code-mixed language models that can better serve the needs of multilingual communities.

To better understand the behavior of Ta$_2$O$_5$ layers in the Ta$_4$O$_{10}$ structure, we were motivated to investigate its base state configuration. However, the complexity of this structure makes it difficult to determine its fundamental characteristics, such as whether it's a correlated insulator or exhibits doped behavior, and the extent to which it exhibits long-range Ta-Ta interaction. We reduced the Ta$_2$O$_5$ layers to a simplified "bird's eye view" representation, focusing on the arrangement of Ta and O atoms in a $1\times 1$ $\alpha$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ cell. Using this model, we performed DFT+U calculations to obtain potential energy surfaces and Monte Carlo simulations to study the long-range Ta-Ta interaction and magnetic behavior. Our results show that the layers are weakly coupled through Ta-Ta interactions, and these interactions cause a shift of about 50meV in the Fermi level. Our findings also indicate that the Ta$_2$O$_5$ layers are doped rather than being in a long-range correlated state, which is consistent with experimental observations. Our study highlights the importance of considering the effects of Ta-Ta interactions when interpreting experimental data, and it demonstrates that the $\alpha$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ layers can serve as an example of a $d$-orbital based 5-fold degenerate Fermi surface within a 2D plane. To further investigate the behavior of Ta$_2$O$_5$ layers, we performed Monte Carlo simulations using a 6-band $d$-orbital Hamiltonian to study the effects of disorder and different levels of Ta-Ta interaction on the electronic and magnetic behavior of Ta$_2$O$_5$ layers. Our results show that even at the edge of a single layer, the presence of Ta-Ta interactions leads to non-Fermi liquid behavior when temperature is comparable to the average level of disorder. Our study also demonstrates that increasing the level of disorder can lead to a non-monetary transition from a non-Fermi liquid state to a magnetic or an insulating state, and that the type of transition depends on the amount of disorder and the level of Ta-Ta interaction. In contrast, our proposed method automates assessment through a scripted dialogue, using a structured set of scenarios that evaluates multiple aspects of the bot's performance in a controlled environment. Cross-domain recommendation has been widely used in recent years, especially in e-commerce platforms that frequently see users switch between different domains. Unfortunately, most existing methods overlook the inherent differences between domains and simply aggregate recommendations without differentiating treatment. This paper argues that such a one-size-fits-all approach may not yield satisfactory results, as it fails to consider the unique features of each domain. A novel framework called MSD-CRR is proposed, one that accounts for the distinct characteristics of source and target domains by identifying their own feature representations and assigning distinct weights to influence the predicted ratings. MSD-CRR has been proven to yield superior performance in numerous scenarios, as validated by extensive empirical testing. As a result, it easily surpasses competing baseline methods in various settings, including recommendation for users who have made no previous transactions. MSD-CRR has been made available on https://github.com/zhongzhongru/msd-crr.

We have developed the Hypatia.jl library to automatically solve conic formulations involving MOSEK's PSDT functions. This package provides a straightforward and efficient way to create conic formulations from polynomial expressions, allowing us to generate and solve conic representations of various organic functions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by creating and solving conic formulations for a range of common functions, including ReLU, Lebesgue, and Brelu, among others. Furthermore, we compare these results to conventional global optimization methods using the NiceSimple function as an example, and find that using Hypatia.jl leads to a significant reduction in solution time. This development enables users of MOSEK to leverage the speed and efficiency of its solver for a broad category of piecewise functions, and provides a starting point for future extensions to the Hypatia.jl library. This development is relevant to a range of applications including artificial neural networks, mixed-integer convex optimization, and global optimization. The Hypatia.jl library is available as an open-source Julia package on the JuliaHub repository under the MIT license. It can be installed using the Julia package manager using the command: julia> using Pkg; Pkg.add("Hypatia")

Artificial intelligence-based neural networks are being successfully applied to automatically diagnose medical conditions and enhance MRI images. However, there's a lack of robust knowledge regarding how to generalize MRI image analysis models to unfamiliar clinical sites without compromising patient safety. This issue is particularly pronounced in regards to image quality assessment, where a model must be able to accurately identify both normal and abnormal images across multiple types, including MRI modality, anatomy, and image acquisition parameters. Furthermore, models must be able to generalize to new sites even after reconfiguration. This study demonstrates the challenges of MRI image analysis model generalization through a dataset containing over 7000 images from eight different MRI modalities, analyzed for noise levels by seven different neural network-based models. The results show that the most advanced neural network-based models, despite being highly accurate, struggle with dimensionality and fail to generalize effectively to new sites, whereas more fundamental models like decision trees are more successful in this regard. This finding implies that even the most sophisticated models may not necessarily excel in complex tasks like MRI image analysis, and that more emphasis should be placed on evaluating their generalizability. This research also presents multiple strategies for enhancing the generalizability of models, leading to an improvement in performance from an average of 0.35 to 0.85 in dimensionality. This finding has significant implications for the development of MRI image analysis models that can be safely transferred to different clinical sites. We investigate a scenario with $n$ binary independent random variables $X_1,...,X_n$ that are defined as $X_i = Y_iZ_i$ where $Y_i$ and $Z_i$ are independent and identically distributed random variables with the property that their squared correlation is less than one, and we show that the concentration of $X_i$ around its expected value is directly proportional to the variance of $Z_i$ and the squared difference of $Z_i$'s expected value from one. This discovery leads to a specific formula that expresses the ratio of a particular $Z_i$'s variance to the sum of all $Z_i$'s variances in terms of the ratio of a particular $X_i$'s variance to the sum of all $X_i$'s variances. This formula can be viewed as a variant of Menger's theorem and has implications for random vectors, linear transformations, and orthogonal matrices. Furthermore, we derive an interesting consequence related to the diversity of binary random vectors when only one of their components is observed. This study also discusses earlier works by Bhatia, Davis, and Dilworth, by Menger, by Rudin, and by Diaconis and Freedman. Finally, we outline two possible extensions of our results. This research was inspired by Dilworth's conjecture regarding the Menger's theorem for binary random variables and its generalization to positive semidefinite matrices. This conjecture was solved by Bhatia, Davis, and Dilworth, but only under the condition of independence between $Y_i$ and $Z_i$, but not necessarily identically distributed. This solution led to the discovery of a concentration inequality, but our current investigation shows that this inequality is more robust and holds without the condition of independence between $Y_i$ and $Z_i$. The recent introduction of incompatible kidney transplants from living donors has provided a significant opportunity to address organ shortages. However, these transplants require highly complex management, including the use of immunosuppressive drugs to control rejection and side effects, and dialysis treatment for patients with end-stage renal disease. Incompatible transplants from living donors pose a greater risk of rejection and complications compared to compatible transplants, and as such, have specific pre- and post-transplant requirements. These requirements vary based on the degree of incompatibility, with options including the use of anti-CD25 or anti-CD19 antibodies to reduce rejection risk, and different doses of immunosuppressive medication to control side effects and kidney function. Despite these challenges, incompatible transplants from living donors have been shown to significantly extend the survival of patients with end-stage renal disease, and can be safely performed with minimal long-term impact on daily life. In this review, we will discuss the pre- and post-transplant assessment, selection, and management of incompatible kidney transplants from living donors, as well as the various immunosuppressive protocols used, and the associated risks and complications. We will also examine the current guidelines and available evidence on this topic, and discuss the ideal patient profile and protocol for these transplants. In addition, we will explore some of the novel approaches being developed to manage these transplants, including the use of gene-edited pigs as a source of compatible kidneys. With over 6,000 patients awaiting kidney transplants in Canada alone, and more than 100,000 worldwide, the opportunity to use incompatible kidney transplants from living donors could help address the shortage of available organs for transplantation. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word embeddings used in a recent study by Loughran-McDonald et al., who incorporated a binary classification model based on the distribution of polar language. We found that the embeddings' high performance rates are largely a result of the classes' inherent distinction, and word embeddings have difficulty distinguishing many polar words from their neutral counterparts, indicating their classification abilities are not as sophisticated as previously suggested. Additionally, we discovered that the task of distinguishing between negative and opposite words, which share the same semantic meaning, is challenging even for the latest language models, and that our proposed an the approach to demarcating the negative and opposite classes by analyzing the distribution of synonyms can be a useful tool for capturing the nuances of polar language. Furthermore, we extracted a subset of words that exhibit varying levels of polarity, which may be employed in models aiming to capture the gradations of polar language. Our results have significant implications for any applications relying on the complexity of word embeddings, and highlight the difficulty of many tasks in natural language processing, which may be both a strength and a weakness of the field. Moreover, our findings suggest that the task of capturing the nuances of polar language may be a simpler version of other natural language processing tasks, which can serve as a benchmark for more complex tasks. This research introduces a hybrid level-set / embedded boundary method to resolve problems related to melting and freezing in solids. By integrating level-set and embedded boundary techniques, we've developed a numerical strategy that utilizes structured grids and achieves a second-order accuracy for fluid flow simulations. A conserved form of the conservation equations is maintained using the conservative level-set method. To address issues related to interface thinning and freezing, we've developed a new approach that prevents the formation of singularities at interfaces and handles freezing problems by introducing a thin layer where the material changes state. This model has been applied to problems involving melting and freezing and has been compared to other numerical methods, demonstrating its effectiveness. To illustrate the method's potential, we've also simulated a melting steel plate problem and a Stefan problem with a complex geometry. To solve the conservation equations, the numerical scheme employs a low-storage, third-order accurate Runge-Kutta time-stepping method and a combination of Godunov's and Lax-Friedrichs flux splitting for the spatial resolution, which allows for the simulation of problems involving large changes in the grid geometry. In multiagent competitions, an equilibrium is considered an optimal strategy for players to converge towards, but most existing methods assume that players' actions are determined by learned policies rather than rational decisions. This work addresses the fundamental question of how players, assumed to be rationally choosing their actions, can be taught to converge to a rationalizable Nash equilibrium in a game through reinforcement learning. We propose a new approach, combining a simple exploration technique with a robust rationality-checking method, has several notable advantages. Firstly, it guarantees convergence to a rationalizable Nash equilibrium in games with single-peaked payoffs under various exploration methods. Secondly, we establish that many existing algorithms can be framed within our general framework, thereby ensuring that they produce a rationalizable Nash equilibrium in games with single-peaked payoffs. Finally, our proposed approach can be applied to a wide range of contexts, including reinforcement learning, by utilizing our general framework as a blueprint for performance monitoring and robust regularization, which enables the production of a rationalizable Nash equilibrium in games with single-peaked payoffs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach through a range of experiments, including ones with large multiplayer games. Lastly, we outline a theoretical analysis to facilitate further understanding, specifically for the proposed exploration method used in conjunction with reinforcement learning. A key factor in preventing the spread of an epidemic in a connected network is the identification of robust core components and vulnerable boundary areas. Research has shown that networks with a distinct boundary, created through processes like phase separation or percolation, are more resilient to epidemics than those without such boundaries. However, these protective effects come at a cost, as they often create bottlenecks that hinder information or disease spread. To explore the interplay between a network's defensive strategies and the spread of an epidemic, we introduce a simple model where links between individuals are randomly replaced at a constant rate once they become infected. This model results in networks that develop distinct boundaries, specifically a "shell structure," and we're interested in examining how the spread of an epidemic is affected by different defensive strategies and various graph configurations. To this end, we'll investigate how the epidemic's impact is influenced by factors such as the rate of link replacement, different shell structures, and the network's overall complexity. This will be achieved through a combination of numerical simulations and theoretical analysis, enabling us to extract general principles from the complex dynamics of the model. Ultimately, our analysis provides a framework for understanding the protective effects of distinct boundary networks and sheds light on the intricate relationships between the epidemic's spread and the networks' defensive mechanisms. This will be reflected in the results, which demonstrate how the epidemic's impact can be either delayed or accelerated through various defensive strategies and how the shell structure formed initially influences the outcome of the epidemic. This in turn will be compared to the initial state of the network before the epidemic struck, offering valuable insights for future studies. reSearch group, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to break down large-scale
projects into manageable tasks, assign them to team members, and track the

allows administrators to define tasks across the wiki and have users with the
'Task Tracker' permission assign articles to these tasks. As a result, users
with the 'Task Tracker' permission can see a list of assigned articles for each

review. This list can be further customized to include columns for various
criteria such as the user who started the article, the user who needs to
review it, and more. This functionality is particularly beneficial for open-source
wiki projects like Wikipedia, research collaborations, and student projects.
It is also highly adaptable, as demonstrated by its successful integration into
McMaster University's reSearch group wiki, a large research collaboration
known as 'wikidata-rdfstore'. It is worth noting that WorkingWiki is now an
inactive project, and its code is no longer being actively maintained by its
original developers. Nonetheless, its source code remains available on GitHub

For any given sentence, there are numerous possible semantic shifts, ranging from very subtle to extremely distant. When analyzing the variety of possible shifts, we find that only a limited set, primarily related to pragmatics, appears to be frequent and significant. Utilizing a specially designed dataset with graded semantic labels, this study demonstrates that the most common shifts are indeed closely tied to pragmatics and that the distribution of shifts is uneven, with the majority being quite similar. To evaluate the capabilities of NLI systems, we created a tailored evaluation method that focuses on the most common and important shifts, and our findings suggest that these systems excel at capturing these frequent shifts but struggle with the rare ones, and that the relationship between NLI tasks and semantic shifts is more complex than previously understood. By exploring the relationship between BERT's output and these shifts, as well as through analysis of evaluation case studies, we gain a deeper insight into the strengths and weaknesses of these systems. Ultimately, this study provides a foundation for investigating the complex nature of semantic variety in discourse. The critical parameter for influencing the performance of large language models has been disputed, with recent research indicating that the hidden state size might be more significant than the token embedding dimension. This study's novel finding reveals that the former indeed surpasses the latter in models of various types, including transformer, linear transformer, and recurrent networks. By optimizing hidden state sizes while maintaining fixed token embedding dimensions, our results show a 2.5-fold improvement in efficient CPU implementation for LLMs. When the hidden state is set at 2048 instead of 4096, a 12-fold decrease occurs in memory usage, allowing a significant increase in the size of models that can be trained on limited resources. When the hidden state is set at 1024, the performance of CPU-based models accelerates 2.5 times, allowing for the training of large models like TAPAS on 64 gigabytes of RAM. When the hidden state is set at 512 instead of 1024, the model's efficiency increases 2.5 times, enabling the training of models like TAPAS on 16 gigabytes of RAM. The most remarkable advancement arises from our novel "degrade" methodology, which yields a 2.5-fold improvement in efficient CPU implementation for LLMs, allowing the efficient CPU-based model TAPAS to be trained on just 8 gigabytes of RAM. In conventional robot networks, many tasks require collaborative automation, but most existing strategies assume robots can freely share information and execute tasks, which is not the case in many real-world scenarios. This research focuses on conventional robot networks where multiple mobile agents can collaborate to complete multi-robot tasks under time and spatial constraints by targeting specific assets. Unlike static targets, mobile assets can move and must be physically reached by robots to complete tasks, presenting new challenges. To overcome these difficulties, this work develops two collaborative schemes using simple robots that can optimize asset movement in an uncertain environment. Simulation results show both methods can efficiently find solutions comparable to those found by unrestricted robots, demonstrating the potential of conventional robot networks in various applications. Moreover, both schemes offer comparable performance at a lower cost, making them suitable for real-world implementations. This research also provides a theoretical analysis of the worst-case scenario performance, setting a baseline for future optimisation strategies. By redefining conventional robot networks as problem domains, this work enables future development of general-purpose learning-based solutions to tackle various asset-targeted automation challenges. While ensuring data remains secure, researchers have been studying how attackers can manipulate educational platforms' instructions and models to leak private student information, and how they can design such attacks to obtain specific data categories, like ability tests, that are difficult to acquire otherwise. By investigating these kinds of attacks on educational platforms, and exploring ways to counter them, the paper aims to address key security concerns in this field. Additionally, the paper provides a discussion on future directions for such attacks and potential countermeasures. By studying these kinds of attacks on educational platforms in a federated setting, the paper hopes to contribute to addressing key security concerns and obtaining valuable student information, and to offer guidance on designing such attacks and countermeasures. Deep neural networks have consistently outperformed traditional methods in various tasks, yet the underlying reason for their success remains poorly understood. One attempt to gain insight into this success is the work on neural network attributes in the frequency domain, which has been effective in simplifying neural networks while maintaining their performance. This paper introduces a new attribute called Random Fourier Features (RFF) to estimate a kernel matrix, a fundamental component in neural networks, and demonstrates its efficacy on several classification problems. RFF offers several advantages over the kernel matrix, including computational efficiency, the ability to be trained end-to-end, and significant memory savings. By substituting the kernel matrix with RFF in a neural network, we achieve comparable performance to the original network, as evidenced by the results obtained. These results show that, in many cases, neural networks with RFF perform significantly better than the original network when input dimensionality is large, and demonstrate the potential of RFF as a general feature extractor. This network can be trained using standard stochastic optimization techniques and has been applied to real data sets without difficulty. This work also highlights the connection between RFF and the bootstrapping method used to train support vector machines. Lastly, this paper provides a theoretical analysis of the generalization error of neural networks with RFF, which sheds further light on the reasons for their effectiveness. This is particularly notable because it makes neural networks with RFF well-suited for real-world data, as they always are compared to other methods. This paper also presents the reader with an overview of the underlying principles, starting from the fundamentals of neural networks, Fourier analysis, and the principles of kernel methods. This is intended to make the paper's results easier to understand for a broader audience. This network has been applied to real data sets, as demonstrated by the results obtained, which show that neural networks with RFF exhibit comparable performance to the original network when input dimensionality is medium-sized, and significantly better performance when the input dimensionality is large. This network has also been compared to the original network, as well as to the network obtained after feature map approximation using random Fourier features, and to the network obtained after approximate kernel matrix computation using the Nyström method. This paper consists of six sections. The first section provides an overview of neural networks, Fourier analysis, and kernel methods, which are the underlying principles of this network. The second section introduces the Random Fourier Features (RFF) attribute and demonstrates its efficacy on several classification problems. The third section presents the results obtained when this network was applied to real data

This achievement is significant as it resolves the issue posed by Hill in 2010 and surpasses the earlier achievement of Quillen from 1980. This extension also allows us to reprove and expand on previous results, including those of Reeve, Hill, and Quillen. Lastly, our study and methodological framework are applicable to a broader and more general context, which we call the Context of Ring Extension Inevitability, defined by specific conditions on the group's representation space. This paper examines conformally developed hypersurfaces within the (n+2)-dimensional sphere, defining a specific function, the M\"obius scalar curvature inflexibility, which varies based on these surfaces and their surrounding environment. It is proven that conformally flat hypersurfaces have a constant M\"obius scalar curvature inflexibility, which differentiates them from another class of surfaces with curved environments. It is also demonstrated that these surfaces have the highest M\"obius scalar curvature inflexibility among all conformally developed hypersurfaces. This leads to the conclusion that conformally flat hypersurfaces have the maximum M\"obius scalar curvature inflexibility, which can be viewed as the mean curvature changing sign. This in turn results in the surfaces being parabolic, and in higher dimensional spaces, this means the surfaces have a specific complex conjugate symmetric structure. This structure can also be achieved through other means, allowing the definition of the M\"obius scalar curvature inflexibility to be broadened to include the (n+1)-dimensional sphere, hyperbolic space, and the flat space of n+1 dimensions. This definition can further be generalized to the hypersurfaces within these spaces, providing the example of the hyperbolic hypersurfaces with curved environments. This in turn results in the conclusion that these hyperbolic hypersurfaces have the maximum M\"obius scalar curvature inflexibility among all conformally developed hypersurfaces within the hyperbolic space of n+1 dimensions. Researchers are considering the challenge of managing interference in large-scale MIMO networks and have investigated the effectiveness of XL-MIMO technology. One key aspect of XL-MIMO involves examining the non-intersecting visibility areas of base stations to reduce co-channel interference. However, as the number of base stations increases, their visibility areas may intersect, which could lead to increased co-channel interference and diminished performance gains from XL-MIMO. This study analyzed the conditions and shapes of visibility areas in an XL-MIMO network using a stochastic access protocol and derived mathematical expressions for the probability of two base stations' visibility areas not intersecting. By leveraging these expressions, we can determine the probability of one base station's visibility area not enclosing another, and in turn, calculate the probability of reduced co-channel interference, thus providing a performance metric for the network. Through numerical computations, we can explore the relationship between performance gains and the number of base stations in an XL-MIMO network. By simulating a 3.5 GHz frequency band, we found that a general condition for non-intersecting visibility areas results in an excessive demand for antennas, whereas an alternative condition could support a greater number of base stations with fewer antennas, thus leading to performance gains near those of large-scale MIMO networks with random access protocol. Furthermore, this study confirmed that the shape of visibility areas serves as the primary factor influencing the probability of reduced co-channel interference and performance gains, and that an alternative condition could support base stations with a hexagonal configuration in an XL-MIMO network, though only if the number of base stations is significantly reduced. This research was conducted without considering the effects of shadowing, stochastic geometry, and random placements of base stations, thus providing a foundation for further investigations into this subject. This study was published in the proceedings of the 2020 IEEE International Conference on Communications, Control, and Computing Technologies.

While neural language models have significantly outperformed $N$-gram models in many applications, they have been surpassed in another area: $N$-gram's effectiveness in pre-training neural models before fine-tuning on specific tasks. This phenomenon can be observed in tasks like machine translation, where neural models are often trained using large corpora without any connection to the target language. This work explores the idea that neural models can be trained on general knowledge with a focus on specific tasks in mind, achieving comparable performance to models trained on massive datasets. This is demonstrated in QADoc, an open-domain question-answering task, where training neural models with a massive corpus led to a 6% reduction in accuracy when compared to the current state-of-the-art. Furthermore, this work proposes a novel approach called ResNet, which incorporates a neural network that corrects the models' outputs without requiring the models to access previous questions. This approach has been applied to both the $N$-gram-based training method and QADoc, resulting in performance improvements. This research is available at https://github.com/ghrghkghr/NgramIsBack.

Moreover, SADRNet demonstrated superior performance when evaluated using a range of challenging real-world datasets, including those with limited-angle and heavily occluded images, face reconstructions, and videos. A growing number of electricity end-users are equipping their homes with smart home energy management systems that include storage units. These systems enable users to balance supply and demand for electricity across different time bands. In a distributed setting, each user independently decides whether to acquire a storage unit, how to program it, and how to manage their electricity consumption. Researchers have studied various self-optimization strategies for individual users, but the impact of self-optimization on collective efficiency in a distributed market has yet to be addressed. This paper explores how storage self-planning affects social welfare in a specific context and demonstrates a method for evaluating the impact. Furthermore, this paper shows that, under certain conditions, adhering to a conservative approach when deciding whether to acquire storage can lead to improved social welfare. Researchers have used smaller datasets to quickly achieve high performance in numerous learning tasks. This efficiency has led some to believe that smaller datasets are inherently better for learning general representations, citing the example of ImageNet. However, this assumption overlooks the unique characteristics of ImageNet, a dataset that, after being scaled down from its original 2.5 million images, comprises 14 million randomly selected images from the Internet, with most being poorly classified. In response, we've developed a new approach, dynamic learning, which leverages a massive dataset with limited class labels by using a separate set of labeled samples for each learning stage. We've applied this method to the ImageNet dataset and achieved superior results in comparison to other comparable models. In particular, our approach exceeded the performance of a model trained on 2.5 million labeled images, achieving 32.8% top-k accuracy with just 1.2 million labeled images. Furthermore, our method demonstrated substantial gains in various learning tasks, including transfer learning, by simply employing a massive dataset with minimal labels. In addition to its advantages in comparison to conventional models, dynamic learning has a more nuanced understanding of the ImageNet dataset, revealing that its effectiveness stems from the dataset's massive magnitude, rather than its specific contents. In essence, our results suggest that smaller datasets are better for learning general representations, a notion we've termed the magnitude hypothesis. To validate this hypothesis, we reduced the scale of ImageNet from 14 million to 280 thousand images and found that, although it was less effective, the reduced dataset still excelled at learning high abstraction levels with 20% to 30% lower performance compared to a dataset of 400 thousand images. In contrast, a comparable model trained on a much smaller dataset of 50 thousand images exhibited 50% to 60% lower performance. Consequently, our research has a dual impact, showcasing the superiority of dynamic learning as well as validating the magnitude hypothesis through a comprehensive set of experiments. In the process, we've developed a new framework for evaluating the efficacy of learning from massive datasets, along with a straightforward, effective method for learning from datasets of any scale, known as the dynamic learning curve. In this work, we explore the potential benefits of using Hamiltonian Neural Networks to provide gradients for various optimization tasks. By interpreting gradients as differential coordinates, we can apply Hamiltonian Neural Networks to output these gradients. To demonstrate the capabilities of this method, we use HNN to approximate gradients in three optimization scenarios. However, our findings reveal that when compared to using the optimizer's standard gradient, incorporating derived gradients via HNN yields inferior results. To address this issue, we propose a straightforward correction strategy, building on the dynamics of the Hamiltonian system. By applying this correction, our results show that using HNN's gradients either surpasses or, in some cases, is on a par with the conventional optimizer, while often achieving this at a lower computational cost. Moreover, this method is capable of generating the optimal solution for specific, well-defined problems, which serves as a unique contribution from this work. To facilitate further research, we have made the code for this project publicly available. Additionally, we pose an open question concerning the absence of noise in the outputs produced by HNN, which could provide valuable insights for both the fields of Hamiltonian Neural Networks and optimization. To back up our findings, we have included a comprehensive set of numerical data obtained through simulations. This includes specific details on the problems we solved, as well as a comprehensive breakdown of the parameters used in each simulation. This data can be found in the appendix to this paper. We establish a well-defined invariant, denoted as $J_0$, for an expansive class of smooth flows on the compact, orientable 3-dimensional manifold $T^2 \times I$, where $T^2$ represents a genus 2 surface. This invariant exhibits properties similar to those observed in volume conjecture, specifically it treats surfaces with integer lengths as special cases, displays additivity over unions of distinct surfaces, and maintains stability under certain partial mergers. Furthermore, $J_0$ is capable of differentiating between two surface types that are dynamically distinct and cannot merge. These findings are supported by numerical data generated through intensive computations. The development of $J_0$ relies on the application of complex analytical techniques to achieve an expression for $J_0$ in terms of an invariant known as $4\Delta$, which was previously established by Mortier for surfaces with integer lengths. The volume hypothesis conjecture is also discussed as a broader context for $J_0$ and $4\Delta$. The proposed $J_0$ can be seen as a precursor to an even more comprehensive invariant, in question form as the volume hypothesis conjecture. The development of $J_0$ also provides an expression for $4\Delta$ that can be used for surfaces with non-integer lengths, which may have important implications for the volume hypothesis conjecture. The numerical computations presented in this study are made possible by a significant reduction in computational requirements, allowing for the efficient simulation of surface evolution and the development of an efficient algorithm for determining the index of surface knots. To accomplish Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD), it is necessary to differentiate between words with the same spelling but varying meanings.  One approach involves using a thesaurus to identify glosses from a lexical knowledge base, then selecting the most appropriate one based on a sentence's context. One such method, using the BBN Context Selection Algorithm, chooses the most suitable gloss by ranking entries according to a score that reflects how well a gloss fits a sentence. However, this technique struggles with a significant issue: the vast majority of words lack a thesaurus definition. To tackle this challenge, a new strategy called Context-gloss Enhancement aims to derive definitions for words without a thesaurus definition by extracting them from sentences that feature the target word in a suitable context.  Once obtained, these definitions can be used to enhance the BBN Context Selection Algorithm, thereby boosting the WSD performance. Experimental results, conducted on a subset of the Senseval-2 dataset featuring the WordNet lexicon, show that Context-gloss Enhancement leads to a notable improvement in F-score by approximately 12% when compared to a state-of-the-art approach, and a 7% gain when compared to the BBN Context Selection Algorithm. Additionally, it was discovered that Context-gloss Enhancement can be effectively applied to words with a thesaurus definition, resulting in an average F-score gain of 3%.  One such instance was observed during the experiment where an average F-score gain of 10% was achieved for words with the Merriam-Webster thesaurus definition. One possible extension of this research involves combining Context-gloss Enhancement with other WSD methods to achieve an even greater performance gain. One such method, the KNN algorithm, was found to be particularly suitable for this purpose as it was discovered during the experiment. One possible issue with this approach, however, is that it may lead to overfitting as was observed during the experiment when Context-gloss Enhancement was applied to the KNN algorithm. One possible solution to this problem, however, is simple and was discovered during the experiment: using a reduced set of definitions. One such instance was observed during the experiment where using a reduced set of definitions resulted in a performance gain of 15% when compared to using the full set of definitions. Our research investigates the feasibility of identifying the charge of top quarks in proton-nucleus collisions using the ALICE detector at the CERN Large Hadron Collider. To achieve this, we examine the decay patterns of top quark-antiquark pairs into $B$-hadrons in our detection range. Account is taken for the effects of $B$-hadron interactions with matter, as well as the influence of charm quark charges, which could potentially misclassify the charge of top quarks. A sample of 100 $\text{pb}^{-1}$ of data at a 5.02 TeV proton-lepton collision rate is assumed for the study, which utilizes a trigger event selection based on high-transverse momentum muons or direct $B$-hadron detection. According to our findings, the charge of top quarks can be reliably determined with up to 60% accuracy, which would rise to approximately 80% with the addition of forward scintillating detectors that could provide more precise $B$-hadron directionality. This, in turn, could further advance our understanding of QCD by revealing the distinct characteristics of quark-gluon plasma formed through the interaction of high-speed protons and heavy nuclei. This could be accomplished at the current LHC settings and would also facilitate future research at the future High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider. We've developed a comprehensive quantum hydrodynamic model to describe interacting Bose systems, and have successfully applied it to simulate the dynamics of a Bose-Einstein condensate under one-dimensional obstacles and also to the annihilation reaction-diffusion process, both in one and two dimensions. Our model's phase-space random approach allows it to accurately capture the behavior of quantum fluctuations, even when the hydrodynamic approach is valid, and has been compared to experimental data and numerical renormalization group calculations, revealing a high level of consistency. An organization's search data is often used to infer employees' information needs and tailor the intranet to their preferences. However, customizing search results can lead to a phenomenon known as 'filter bubble,' where users are isolated from other relevant information. To investigate this effect, we conducted a search for two high-profile news articles on Google at two points in time and measured the percentage of users who would see the same headline on the front page of Google. We found that Google's search algorithms conceal the same headline from users with different query histories. As a result, the same search yields different answers for the same query depending on user-specific data, and customizations can cause users to miss important information. Our findings highlight the magnitude of this effect, demonstrating that search results can vary significantly (up to 42%) and that customizations can lead to a substantial decrease (as much as 92%) in users seeing the same headline. These results underscore the significance of considering the 'filter bubble' effect in the context of intranet search. By examining our data under different customization levels, we can gain insight into how search algorithms behave and provide a basis for evaluating the extent to which users are isolated from information by the search system. Our research also offers a novel perspective on the issue of search result diversity, which can be applied to intranet search. By calculating the amount of pertinent information users may overlook due to customization levels, our findings provide a framework for evaluating the extent to which search systems restrict users' access to information and can be used to guide development of diversity algorithms that take account of the context. The remote control of a single-point Laser Doppler Velocimeter (LDV) system to achieve two-dimensional velocity measurements in an object under investigation has been a long-standing challenge. To overcome this limitation, researchers have relied on the system's inherent properties being linear and having a single control point. However, for many complex applications, these assumptions are not met, rendering the system difficult to use. This paper addresses this issue by presenting a distant control method for a single-point LDV system. By generating a non-contact reference beam using a beam splitter and a mirror placed near the measurement point, the system's sensitivity to target characteristics is significantly reduced. Furthermore, the paper provides a mathematical framework for controlling the system and recovering the scattered light pattern. As a result, the system's response surface can be accurately reconstructed, enabling the recovery of two-dimensional velocity measurements. Experimental validation has been conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of this method. By generating a sample beam pattern and recovering the corresponding velocity distribution, the accuracy of the system has been assessed. The results show that the system's response can be precisely predicted, recovering the velocity distribution with an error of less than 5%. This method has been applied to measure the velocity distribution in a turbulent jet, yielding recoverable results with an error of less than 10%. This distant control method for a single-point LDV system paves the way for the two-dimensional control of a wide range of applications, including turbulence, combustion, and chemical reactions, among others. This method has been made available on the website of the Laboratoire de Mécanique et Énergétique at the University of Poitiers.

In this work, we introduce a new computational framework called "executable regular functions for infinite sequences". This innovative concept draws inspiration from Alan Turing's initial idea of a computer, and we believe it has significant potential benefits, especially in dealing with problems related to computability regarding infinite data sets. A key aspect of this technology are "recognizers" - essentially the equivalent of Turing machines that can process infinite sequences - and we can program them to perform various tasks, and even execute subroutines, on a vast array of sequences, including those generated randomly, naturally, or artificially. We have successfully implemented this concept on a specific sequence and it has notable implications for certain related problems. In addition, we outline a strategy for converting certain types of regular functions into this format, which in turn has significant repercussions for related challenges. In the course of this research, we also discovered a few interesting regular functions that, to the best of our knowledge, have not been reported on before. We have discovered three fundamental properties that this structure inherits from the lattice of subgroups of a Galois group under the Weyl criterion. Additionally, we have established connections between boolean involutive structures and the fundamental group of a hyperbolic manifold, as well as a classification of these structures within the lattice of subgroups of a Galois group. Furthermore, we have developed an iterative procedure for constructing boolean involutive structures and demonstrated its applicability to hyperbolic manifolds with loop parabolic fundamental group. This involves a boolean extension of Birkhoff's theorem, providing an ordering of the elements of a lattice that maintains the preservation of the initial properties of the boolean operation. Researchers employed a two-step method to analyze the elemental abundance patterns of approximately 74,000 stars within the Milky Way's disk by removing signatures of chemical enrichment and variations in rotation, then re-analyzing data from the APOGEE-2. By removing the effects of chemical enrichment, they were able to map how elements such as iron, carbon, and magnesium were distributed throughout the galaxy. This allowed them to create detailed images of how certain elements were incorporated into stars and how the galaxy's abundance patterns evolved over time. By removing the impact of variations in rotation, they were able to determine the ages of stars by analyzing the abundance patterns of elements like aluminum and sodium, which are produced at higher rates in certain low-mass stars with slower rotations. This helped them identify distinct populations of stars that had similar ages, were located at the same distance from the galaxy's center, but had different velocities and were moving in different directions. This analysis revealed that the galaxy's disk contained multiple populations with different ages, were located at different distances from the center, and were moving in different directions, which was not previously known. This information will be useful for understanding the galaxy's evolution, how it formed, and how its stars moved to their current positions. This research also identified areas of the galaxy that were missing certain populations of stars, which could be the result of the galaxy's interaction with nearby stars or the presence of a bar at its center. This will be important for further research into the galaxy's evolution, as well as the formation of stars and the movement of the galaxy's matter. This research used data from the APOGEE-2 for approximately two years, and the resulting images and information about the galaxy's abundance patterns are available online. The rapid spread of digital rumors in China has a significant impact on public health, economy, and social stability, as seen in 2020 when COVID-19 cases surged. This research aims to investigate the speed, extent, and influencing factors of China's digital rumor spread, as well as their consequences on individuals and society. Our analysis used a combination of network analysis, machine learning, and empirical data from a large-scale online survey. The results reveal an interesting phenomenon where shorter, negative digital rumors spread quickly but have a limited impact, whereas longer, positive ones spread more extensively but more slowly. Furthermore, we found that digital rumors affecting physical health spread rapidly but have a limited impact, whereas those impacting mental health spread more slowly but have a greater impact. Additionally, we found significant differences in the consequences of digital rumors on individuals with varying ages, occupations, and levels of education. This study contributes to the field of information diffusion by providing insights into the speed and impact of digital rumors, as well as their consequences on individuals and society, which can be applied to similar crises in the future. This research can be useful for developing an early warning system for digital rumors and strategies for managing their spread, which in turn can help mitigate their adverse effects on public health and society. This research can also be used as a basis for comparing the consequences of digital rumors in China with those in other countries. This study has implications for the role of technology in promoting social stability and public health during crises, as well as for the development of effective countermeasures to control the spread of digital rumors. Processing temporal data is crucial in various applications, and stream processing has become a key technology in this process. Although there has been significant progress in processing time-ordered data, research in this field has primarily been focused on instantaneous and historical data processing. In contrast, regular streams, which are fundamental in graph temporal data, have received relatively little attention in terms of efficient processing methods. This study addresses this gap by presenting an optimized algorithm, called 2-phase, for processing regular streams, as well as a corresponding engine called LifeFlow. In comparison to other approaches, the 2-phase algorithm exhibits a notable reduction in computation costs, and LifeFlow demonstrates superior performance in various benchmarks, including a real-world case study. This research also introduces a novel evaluation metric called throughput-overhead, which provides a comprehensive view of efficient data processing. This finding can be beneficial for various contexts, not limited to stream processing. By leveraging the LifeFlow engine source code, other researchers can replicate and build upon this work, as well as explore further development in this area. When training neural networks using supervised learning, it is common to modify standard loss functions for various purposes, such as improving robustness and preventing overfitting. Despite its prevalence, little is known about the effects of loss function modification, particularly under what conditions it impacts the neural network's ability to classify effectively. In our research, we investigate how altering a loss function, specifically a modified version of the cross-entropy loss with added regularization, affects the performance of a neural network. We found that such modifications can result in worse performance, but only in specific situations characterized by large differences between the training and testing data. To achieve better performance, we developed a new, data-dependent bound on the altered loss function, which can be used to minimize performance degradation. By leveraging this bound, we created a set of conditions that guarantee performance remains within a certain level of the optimal performance achieved using the original cross-entropy loss function. To illustrate the usefulness of these conditions, we generated a set of scenarios with diverse levels of data differences and demonstrated that our approach effectively bounds the altered loss function and maintains performance at a high level. To further evaluate our results, we conducted additional experiments using a robustness-aware loss function, which also yielded promising outcomes. Our research provides a framework for analyzing and controlling the effects of loss function modification and can be applied to a wide range of neural network models and various loss function modifications. By developing this framework, we can now confidently declare that modifying loss functions is an instance of instance-dependent data-dependent regularization and assign it a corresponding label in our taxonomy of data-dependent regularization techniques. Our research has been tailored to address real-world purposes, such as training neural networks on imbalanced data, but it can be extended to explore other loss function modifications and, more broadly, other instances of instance-dependent data-dependent regularization. Our findings are validated across a wide range of models and scenarios, but our approach can be applied to other neural network models and loss function modifications, including those mentioned in our discussion of future work, such as adversarial loss functions, loss functions with memory, loss functions for multi-task learning, and more.
