Our analysis of the TMC-1 ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers allows us to accurately quantify the abundances of CCH and CN variants of the cyclopentadiene cycle and determine their vibrational excitation levels. By utilizing a non-linear least squares method, we determined the ethynyl cyclopentadiene's rotational, vibrational, and electric dipole moment coefficients with great precision. Further, we calculated the relative abundances of the two isomers, found the cyclopentadiene CCH abundance to be (2.63±0.24) times $10^{-8}$, determined the ethynyl cyclopentadiene's rotational temperature to be 4.8 K, and found its excitation levels to be (0.35±0.03) or (0.19±0.03) based on the ground or first vibrational state, respectively. By comparing our results with interstellar molecular formation theories, we found that the ethynyl cyclopentadiene's abundance could be explained by atomic collisions, whereas the cyclopentadiene cycle's abundance might be better accounted for through radical recombination. Additionally, we found the TMC-1 ethynyl cyclopentadiene's column density to be (2.05±0.18) times $10^{12}$, the cyclopentadiene cycle's column density to be (6.48±0.58) times $10^{12}$, and determined the TMC-1 ethynyl cyclopentadiene's abundance with respect to cyclopentadiene to be (0.32±0.03) or (0.19±0.03) based on the ground or first vibrational state, respectively. Further study is necessary to validate our findings about the ethynyl cyclopentadiene's abundance with respect to CCH and CN variants of the cyclopentadiene cycle. Further, we propose that ethynyl benzene's abundance could be analogously determined if its transition frequency can be identified. Lastly, if the TMC-1 cloud's age is taken into consideration, then the ethynyl cyclopentadiene's abundance with respect to cyclopentadiene is consistent with the chemical time-scale of the interstellar medium.

In recent years, advances in neural machine translation have been complemented by the development of neural machine interpretation, which generates structured semantic representations from sequence outputs. This approach has been applied to a variety of tasks including machine creation, question answering, and text summarization. However, existing methods typically process one sentence at a time, using a single decoder to produce the next word in the current sentence, without considering the impact on subsequent sentences. In this paper, a novel neural network called NFoC is presented, which employs a dual decoder architecture to produce one sentence at a time, allowing for the optimization of the current sentence to minimize its impact on the subsequent sentence. Experiments conducted on various datasets have demonstrated NFoC's superior performance, with NFoC outperforming the baseline by 2-4% in certain metrics. Additionally, NFoC has been found to be more effective when the relationship between sentences is complex, without incurring a significant computational cost. Experimental results have also shown that NFoC can be applied to both supervised and semi-supervised machine creation, with NFoC's performance being comparable to state-of-the-art methods in the field. Code for NFoC is available at https://github.com/ghrua/NFoC.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) variations, building on the fundamental framework of singular spectrum analysis (SSA). We offer a free online access to our pre-computed spatially-weighted MFSSA eigenobjects for surface temperature variability across the Arctic region from 1981 to 2020, as well as for global sea surface temperature variability over two time spans: 1960-2019 and 1981-2020. By utilizing these eigenobjects within linear regression models, we found significant improvements in predicting Arctic temperature trends and global mean temperature trends. Moreover, our results demonstrate that MFSSA is a more efficient method in comparing to other alternatives such as multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA) and vector autoregression (VAR), especially when dealing with datasets of large spatial dimensions. Consequently, our research is applicable to a broader range of datasets, including but not limited to temperature anomalies in the Arctic region. We've created an image analysis system using W-Net to pinpoint nuclei in histopathology images. By integrating image segmentation, we've developed a two-part network consisting of an encoder and a decoder. First, the encoder distinguishes between nuclei and non-nuclei, and then the decoder identifies specific types of nuclei. We've tested W-Net on images of the liver, pancreas, and lung but had the most success with liver images. When comparing W-Net to another leading method, our system showed a 6.46% improvement in accuracy. Additionally, we've integrated W-Net into a nucleus tracking system that tracks nuclei over time, providing information on how cancers progress. To do this, we've developed a novel way to represent progressive changes graphically. One way to do this is with graph convolutional networks (GCN), however, GCN requires a pre-determined number of time points, which isn't always known in advance, so we've replaced GCN with a simple linear regression to use W-Net. Our results show that this system effectively identifies key changes in cancer progression. The code for this project is available online at github.com/ghrasoul/WNet. The regional converse theorem is proven for specific groups in the positive characteristic case: the odd special orthogonal groups of degree 2k+1 and the symplectic groups of degree 2k+2, under the assumption that a non-rational irreducible character of one of these groups lifts to a character of the absolute Galois group that is rationally attached to the corresponding group over a number field. This result is paired with the previous fact that the groups in question have a large number of irreducible characters, leading to the conclusion that the majority of irreducible characters are defined over the rational numbers. The proof relies on the classification of irreducible characters, the Galois properties of character degrees, and the presence of specific quadratic characters. The result itself is also tied to the question of whether the majority of irreducible characters of the general linear groups in the positive characteristic case are defined over the rational numbers. The proof of the regional converse theorem for these specific groups can be found in [GLM21], with an alternative approach discussed in [LL22]. The term'regional' refers to the fact that the theorem only applies to groups with specific characteristics and a particular level of complexity. The word 'converse' indicates that the theorem connects a particular property (being rationally attached) to another property (being non-rational). In recent years, graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) have gained significant popularity in various tasks, achieving high accuracy and broad applicability, and have been particularly effective in social network analysis, molecular chemistry studies, and traffic flow prediction. However, as GCNNs lack a clear fundamental framework, comparable to conventional convolutional neural networks based on the Fourier transform, this lack of a theoretical foundation has led to confusion among researchers about the underlying properties and working mechanism of GCNNs. This study aims to clarify this ambiguity by providing a novel perspective on GCNNs, framed within a matched filtering theory context, which offers a comprehensive understanding of the networks' core functionality, including spectral convolution, graph attention networks, GCNN filters' behavior, and GCNN layers, ultimately leading to a concise derivation of the average output of a GCNN. By integrating this matched filtering framework into the GCNN architecture, we also propose a simple and efficient data-driven learning method, demonstrating its applicability in modeling complex chemical compounds with graph-based structures. By re-casting GCNNs within this established theoretical framework, we have made the networks' functionality more transparent, facilitating the development of new applications and guiding future research towards more principled design decisions. This work has been submitted to ArXiv. Additionally, due to the generality of the matched filtering framework, we have repurposed its components to design a new learning method, which has been successfully employed in modeling complex chemical compounds with graph-based structures, a challenging task that has been successfully resolved by a more advanced architecture, Reinforcement Learning Graph Attention Network, which has also been submitted to ArXiv. Here, we examine the model's properties under its deformed version and observe its unique features. Elastography, an imaging technique that utilizes pressure waves to assess tissue conditions, has its effectiveness limited due to the tendency of ultrasound waves to deviate from straight paths within the body. This issue causes an inaccurate estimation of tissue stiffness, a major drawback of conventional elastography. To address this problem, researchers have explored and developed new methods based on the assumption that ultrasound waves travel in straight lines. However, these approaches are vulnerable to errors caused by the refraction of ultrasound waves. To address this challenge, our research introduces a novel elastography technique based on the concept of a "virtual origin." By determining the optimal distance between the transducer and the "virtual origin," this method can compensate for refraction-related distortions and elastography estimation inaccuracies. To this end, we developed an algorithm that leverages synthetic aperture technology and robust displacement estimation techniques. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we conducted a series of experiments using a phantom and a real-time elastography technique. The results show that our technique can rectify refraction-related distortions and elastography estimation inaccuracies, both quantitatively and qualitatively. Consequently, this method enhances the precision of elastography estimations, a finding that is also applicable to other imaging modalities that rely on the assumption that ultrasound waves travel in straight lines. To this end, our research has a broader impact on imaging modalities such as photoacoustic imaging. To make the algorithm more efficient, we also explored the possibility of reducing the number of synthetic aperture samples, a feat we achieved by developing an innovative stopping criterion for the algorithm. This stopping criterion, in turn, enabled us to develop a variant of the algorithm that can operate on real-time elastography data. To this end, we conducted a series of experiments that compared the performance of the variant algorithm with the original algorithm, a feat we accomplished by examining the impact of various parameters on the algorithm's performance, including the number of synthetic aperture samples, image matrix size, and image pixel size. The results show that the variant algorithm performs similarly to the original algorithm across a range of parameters, a finding that is also applicable to real-world elastography data. Consequently, this variant algorithm is suitable for a range of imaging applications, including elastography, photoacoustic imaging, and synthetic aperture ultrasound imaging. To tackle this challenge, the "rational" design framework focuses on algorithms in areas such as information retrieval, genetics, and astronomy, among others. By prioritizing a clear and logical structure over efficiency, a natural path to algorithm development is established, one that is underpinned by the principles of deductive reasoning. This approach can be represented through the universal language of propositional logic, which in turn allows us to assess the correctness of algorithms by validating the corresponding deductive arguments, and also to compare their performance by examining the underlying deductive structures. Through this methodology, we have successfully analyzed numerous well-known algorithms, revealing both their inherent limitations as well as areas for their improvement, and have even discovered new variants that surpass the original algorithms. By adopting this "rational" design method, which is inspired by the principles of deductive inference, we can create a library of high-quality algorithms that are both efficient and effective. This approach can be applied to a wide range of problems, not limited to the ones examined in this paper, which includes, for example, problems in biology, finance, and neuroscience, among others. This methodology is versatile and can be used in conjunction with a broad range of programming languages and optimization techniques, such as linear programming, genetic algorithms, and deep learning, among others. This research introduces a novel framework for games that involves both cooperative and competitive elements, which we call "pursuit-withdrawal" games. A key feature of these games is that cooperation is only beneficial when one player is ahead of the other, and it hinders progress when the first player is behind. Another characteristic is that the state of being ahead or behind can change based on the position of the players on a linear hierarchy. Our primary goal is to explore strategies for these games by utilizing a hierarchical framework, and our key discovery shows that players can employ a simple "look-ahead" method that effectively helps us understand the structure of the strategy hierarchy. Furthermore, our model allows us to determine the optimal level of cooperation as well as the level at which one player should aim to gain an advantage over the other, based on the characteristics of the games. In the course of our analysis, we also identified a specific type of hierarchy that we call a "period-two hierarchy," and demonstrated that it is a particular case of the more general hierarchical framework. Our research on these games also yields a significant finding, which is that there is a level of cooperation that results in a period-two hierarchy with two levels, and this level of cooperation is directly related to the distance between the players on the hierarchy. In addition to these results, we provide a detailed example of a period-two hierarchy with three levels, and also offer some general advice on how to design effective cooperation strategies for these types of games. These advice include implementing a linear hierarchy with a specific level of cooperation that is equivalent to a certain distance between the players, and also a level of cooperation that results in one player aiming to gain a certain level of advantage over the other, and finally, a way of determining this level of advantage as well as the distance between the players based on the parameters of the games. These advice enable us to design specific cooperation strategies for any given game, and our results demonstrate that these strategies will always lead to a period-two hierarchy. These research on pursuit-withdrawal games also allows us to frame the "capricious dictator problem" as a particular type of these games, and our results on these games enable us to solve the capricious dictator problem. Our research on pursuit-withdrawal games also allows us to frame the problem of finding an optimal cooperation strategy in a hierarchy that changes over time as a special type of these games, and our results on these games provide us with an efficient method for finding this strategy. Our research involves creating two cutting-edge technology scenarios: model-driven reinforcement learning and reinforcement learning for multiple, unrelated tasks. We carry out a series of experiments using a straightforward grid-world environment and a more complex scenario with multiple tasks. Our findings show that reinforcement learning with models reduces the required training time and boosts performance when switching to new tasks. However, our analysis reveals a significant flaw: if the environment changes substantially, their performance plummets. To overcome this limitation, we develop an independent module for each sub-task, placing our model at the decision-making core. This design enables us to reduce training time and avoid severe performance deterioration when switching to new tasks or changing the environment. Our results highlight the benefits of this design under various conditions and across multiple, unrelated tasks. Our approach also compares favorably to other system designs in our evaluation. Ultimately, our method's efficiency and robustness make it suitable for situations involving complex, dynamic environments and multiple tasks. We create an abstract version of Gödel's first incompleteness theorem by using a specific formalized system, which includes a limited set of basic mathematical statements and is capable of making general assertions about itself. We then generate a "twisted" version of this system, which is able to detect the existence of a specific kind of statement that contradicts itself. The "twisted" system's own incompleteness is demonstrated by showing it is impossible to prove a crucial statement that asserts a specific type of self-referential statement exists, even though this type of statement is readily apparent within the "twisted" system itself. We also show that this self-referential statement is necessarily undecidable within the "twisted" system and cannot be proved or disproved by this system, thus providing a second, stronger form of the Gödel first incompleteness theorem. We then use this "twisted" system to create a sequence of increasingly complex systems, each with its own unique form of incompleteness, showing that it's possible to create systems of any desired level of incompleteness. We also show that these systems are all essentially equivalent to each other, yet are not able to recognize this fact, thus providing a new proof for a significant consequence of Gödel's diagonalization lemma. We end by discussing the implications of these results for certain theories about the nature of reality and knowledge, specifically the concept of "metamathematical reality" proposed by Tarski, and the distinction between abstract truth and physical reality highlighted by Carnap and Tarski. We then consider a system that contains a statement that asserts it is incomplete, yet this statement can be shown to be false, thus demonstrating that it is possible to construct a system that is in a state of "epistemic crisis". We show that all systems like this are essentially equivalent to a specific, well-known undecidable system known as $\omega$-inconsistency, yet the term $\omega$-inconsistency is actually a misnomer, thus providing a new perspective on this concept. This paper formulates the three spheres theorem for non-linear eigenfunctions of a significant part of the Dirac operator, specifically its factorized components, within real analytic functions. We establish this theorem for a substantial portion of the Dirac operator, and its factors, and demonstrate its implications for the Liouville theorem in Clifford analysis. Additionally, we offer a modified three spheres theorem for its components, and identify a significant relationship between them and the original three spheres theorem. Furthermore, we discuss the limitations and the scope of our results, as well as comparing them to analogous theorems in other areas of mathematics. Moreover, we provide a list of open problems related to the three spheres theorem in Clifford analysis. Lastly, we offer a concise overview of the main topics discussed in this paper.

In recent years, GAN-based methods have gained popularity for solving inverse problems in imaging. These challenges require reconstructing an object that is distant from the measurement equipment and is affecting the observed signal. A significant issue with these challenges is the limited dynamic range of the observed signal. This paper proposes a new GAN-based algorithm called CEGAN, which employs a conditional encoder to produce an encoder conditioned on the measurements. This results in better encoded representations when the measurements are noisy, specifically when noise is added to the measurements during training. When applied to noisy measurements during testing, CEGAN yields superior results, outperforming existing encoders and naive conditional encoders, while producing accurate reconstructions, according to quantitative metrics. PSRMs, the pulsar phase-metered arrival measurements, contain valuable information that can be used to understand the interstellar medium. Our research utilized PSRMs from the pulsar B1133+16, observed over 17 years, to study the refractive scintillation of radio waves. Analyzing these measurements, we were able to separate their component variations: pulsar signal changes, emission carrier frequency shifts, and RVM phase variations. After removing these components, we were left with small changes in the signal, likely resulting from the interstellar medium. To better understand these changes, we converted the measurements from the time domain to the frequency domain and studied two specific types of variations: differential scintillation and frequency modulation. Our results showed a wide range of spectral power for the signal variations and distinct components related to differential scintillation and frequency modulation. By comparing our findings with previous research on the same pulsar and on the PSR B1133+16 beam model, we were able to map the signal variations to specific regions of the interstellar medium. Our analysis revealed a narrow band of spectral power for differential scintillation and a much broader range of frequencies for frequency modulation, in addition to uncovering localized variations in the signal and a relation between them and the RVM phase variations. This connection allowed us to create a simplified model that accurately described the signal variations, even after removing the effects of the RVM phase variations. This model also provided us with an estimate of the frequency modulation index and the Doppler shift, which, in turn, gave us the distance to the interstellar medium and the velocity of this medium. This velocity was found to be similar to previous research and the Earth's movement within the Milky Way had a more significant impact on the signal variations than the velocity of the pulsar. This finding was also consistent with previous research on the same pulsar and it supported the idea that the velocity of the Pulsar B1133+16 is much lower than previously estimated, which, in turn, supported the relation between the beam opening angle and the velocity of the pulsar. Recently, neural network-based generative models have achieved a human-like sound quality in speech synthesis, surpassing traditional statistical approaches. In particular, WaveNet has established a new standard with its highly realistic output and extensive applications. However, this model's significant computational requirements and memory usage limit its practical use on high-speed speech synthesis systems. Additionally, the model's lack of pitch control through its convolutional components hinders its capability to produce high-quality audio with a single network. In response to these challenges, this paper presents Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, a novel end-to-end speech generation framework based on WaveNet that overcomes these limitations by integrating a pitch-independent recurrent neural network and a dilated convolution neural network with a fixed pitch range. Recent advancements in graph neural networks have primarily focused on Euclidean-based methods, ignoring the potential benefits of Lorentzian geometry. Our research fills this gap by introducing LGNNs, a novel framework that leverages Lorentzian geometry to enhance graph neural networks. LGNNs incorporate a unique node representation using the Lorentzian metric, allowing for efficient learning of coordinates that minimize the distance between graphs. Our analysis shows that LGNNs optimize a non-Euclidean version of the clustering objective, providing a theoretical foundation for this optimization. We further demonstrate the practical advantages of LGNNs in real-world applications by developing LGNN-based variants of popular neural network architectures, which outperform their non-Lorentzian counterparts in tasks such as node classification and clustering. Moreover, LGNNs can be trained on significantly larger graphs, leading to a new benchmark record in WebSphere. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghaleem/Lorentzian-GCN. Our findings suggest that LGNNs can be a promising alternative to conventional graph neural networks, offering improved performance in various real-world tasks.
